summary.title: Best practices for REST API design
summary.one_liner: You learn practical conventions for designing REST APIs that are easy to consume, secure, performant, and versionable, illustrated with Express.js examples.
keywords: nouns instead of verbs in urls
crud http methods get post put delete
how to design a rest api
takeaways: Use JSON for request and response bodies and set Content-Type to application/json.
Name endpoints with plural nouns and let HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) express the action.
Nest child resources under parents (e.g. /articles/:id/comments), but avoid nesting more than two or three levels deep.
Return standard HTTP status codes and helpful error messages, while avoiding leaking sensitive details; support filtering, sorting, and pagination for large datasets.
Secure APIs with TLS, least-privilege role checks, and cache carefully; version with /v1/, /v2/ prefixes so clients are not broken.
summary.summary: The Stack Overflow Blog article explains how to design REST APIs that are easy to understand, future-proof, secure, and fast. It walks through a list of best practices: JSON request/response handling, noun-based endpoint paths with plural names, logical nesting of resources, standard HTTP error codes, filtering/sorting/pagination via query strings, SSL/TLS and role checks for security, caching, and URL versioning. Each practice is illustrated with short Express.js and body-parser code samples. The article is conceptual and aimed at general web developers rather than a deep dive into any single framework.
